title: English Skill Lab – Listening Full Mock 01

turns.text_en: Good morning, Bramble Clock Workshop, Mara speaking. Has the clock stopped altogether, or is it doing something more complicated? We do repairs here, but I should say at the outset that our first appointment is an inspection, not a promise to replace anything. Some customers are relieved to hear that; others are hoping for a quick fix.

I'm asking about a clock that belonged to my grandmother. It still runs, but the chime is wrong and I don't want to damage the wooden case by trying to fix it myself. I'd like to book an inspection before arranging any expensive work.

It is a mantel clock rather than a tall case clock. The case is small enough to carry, but its brass movement feels surprisingly heavy. My grandmother kept it on a shelf in the sitting room, away from the windows.
That helps. A mantel clock can be handled at the counter, so you won't need our home-collection van. Please keep the hands still while moving it and wrap the glass door separately.
The case is made of walnut, or at least that's what the original note inside says. The finish is a little faded on one side, which is why I want to be careful about using cleaning products.

Walnut is fairly common in clocks from that period. We'll examine the surface but we won't polish or replace anything without your permission, especially if you want to preserve the marks from its age.

The clock keeps reasonable time. The problem is the chime: it sounds two minutes after the hour, and sometimes it strikes twice when it ought to strike only once. I thought the hands were loose, but they seem secure.
Thank you for describing that so precisely. We'll check the striking mechanism first; replacing the whole movement would be unnecessary until we know what's causing the delay.
I was hoping to come on Tuesday, but I've just noticed I have a hospital appointment then. Thursday would be much easier, particularly if someone can look at it during the morning.
Thursday is available. I can hold a counter appointment for you and send a reminder, so there's no need to make a second journey if your plans change.
I could be there just after ten, although the bus from my village is sometimes late. Would ten forty work? That would give me time to walk up from the station without rushing with the clock.
Yes, 10:40 is the appointment time I've recorded. I'll avoid the earlier slot because it's already reserved for a larger instrument.
I saw an old leaflet suggesting the inspection was twenty pounds. Is that still correct? I'd like to know the charge before I bring it in, because I haven't agreed to a repair yet.
The current inspection fee is twenty-eight pounds, not twenty. That covers the written diagnosis and is separate from any restoration work you might authorise later.
Should I put the clock flat in the bottom of my bag? It's quite awkward to hold, and I was worried it might topple over on the journey.
Please keep it upright in a firm box. A folded towel around the sides is fine, but laying the movement on its back could put pressure on the delicate parts.
Could you ring me when you've checked it? I'm at work most afternoons and won't always answer my mobile, so it might be difficult to discuss a price by telephone.
We can send the written estimate by email instead. You can read it when you're free, and nothing will proceed until you explicitly accept it.
I know a full restoration might take a while, but I'm mainly interested in the diagnosis. If I leave it with you on Thursday, when should I expect to hear something useful?
The report normally takes five days. That's for diagnosis, not repair; a new spring or other part could extend the total time if you later decide to proceed.
If I can't get back here in person, may my sister collect it? She works near the workshop and could bring the original receipt and my written authorisation.
Your sister can collect it, provided she brings the receipt and some identification. I've added that arrangement to the booking so colleagues won't be confused.

Before you travel, please take a quick photograph of the face and case. It's useful for our condition record, and it can also help us put the clock back exactly as you remember it. Is there anything else about the booking that I should check?

That makes sense. My grandmother cared about the sound of that clock as much as its appearance, so I'd rather know what is wrong before anyone starts replacing parts. I'll bring the details with me. Thanks, Mara.

questions.prompt_en: How should the client bring the clock?
questions.explanation_vi: **Đáp án A – carried upright in a padded box.** Nhân viên yêu cầu giữ đồng hồ đứng trong hộp chắc, có khăn lót để bảo vệ bộ máy. **B – laid flat inside the travel bag:** Người hỏi đề xuất đặt đồng hồ nằm phẳng trong túi, nhưng nhân viên yêu cầu giữ thẳng đứng và cảnh báo áp lực lên cơ cấu máy. **C – transported without a protective container:** Nhân viên yêu cầu có hộp cứng và khăn đệm quanh đồng hồ, nên không thể mang không có vật bảo vệ. **Bằng chứng:** “Please keep it upright in a firm box. A folded towel around the sides is fine, but laying the movement on its back could put pressure on the delicate parts.”. *Ghi chú: lời giải biên tập có dẫn chứng, còn chờ giáo viên duyệt độc lập.*

questions.prompt_en: How will the estimate be sent?
questions.explanation_vi: **Đáp án A – as an email message.** Nhân viên đề nghị gửi bản báo giá bằng email để khách đọc và xác nhận lúc rảnh. **B – as a letter sent by post:** Không có quyết định gửi thư bưu điện; văn bản được gửi dưới dạng email. **C – as a telephone conversation:** Khách từng đề nghị gọi điện, nhưng họ thường bận buổi chiều nên hai bên chọn email thay cho trao đổi qua điện thoại. **Bẫy nghe hiểu:** Phân biệt phương án khách đưa ra lúc đầu với cách gửi cuối cùng nhân viên xác nhận. **Vị trí bằng chứng:** Part 1, lượt T17, T18. *Lời giải biên tập; chưa được giáo viên xác nhận độc lập.*

questions.prompt_en: When should the customer expect the initial assessment rather than the restoration to be complete?
questions.explanation_vi:
**Đáp án B: about five days for diagnosis.** Khách chỉ hỏi khi có bản chẩn đoán ban đầu. Nhân viên tách rõ thời gian chẩn đoán khoảng năm ngày khỏi toàn bộ thời gian phục chế.

**Dẫn chứng trong transcript** (lượt T19, T20): “I know a full restoration might take a while, but I'm mainly interested in the diagnosis. If I leave it with you on Thursday, when should I expect to hear something useful? The report normally takes five days. That's for diagnosis, not repair; a new spring or other part could extend the total time if you later decide to proceed.”

**Phân tích phương án nhiễu:** **A** (after a same-day counter check) không phải thông tin/kết luận cuối phù hợp với yêu cầu câu hỏi; **C** (only once the full restoration is finished) cũng không được đoạn trích xác nhận là đáp án. So sánh mục tiêu hỏi với kết luận và điều kiện trong lời thoại, không chỉ tìm từ trùng.

**Kỹ năng:** nghe paraphrase, kiểm tra kết luận và loại phương án được nhắc tới nhưng không đúng mục tiêu.

questions.explanation_vi: **Đáp án đúng: A – a family member: the sister.** Câu hỏi: Who will collect the clock after inspection? **Evidence (T21, T22):** “If I can't get back here in person, may my sister collect it? She works near the workshop and could bring the original receipt and my written authorisation. Your sister can collect it, provided she brings the receipt and some identification. I've added that arrangement to the booking so colleagues won't be confused.”. Thông tin cần nghe là **sister**; phương án A tương ứng với kết luận trong đoạn nghe. **Đối chiếu distractors:** B – a colleague from the workshop – không phải câu trả lời cuối cùng theo evidence; C – a neighbour living nearby – không phải câu trả lời cuối cùng theo evidence. Đề cũ chấm sai khóa; giáo viên vẫn phải xác nhận duy nhất đáp án trước khi phát hành.

parts.title: Canal Discovery Day: Visitor Orientation

turns.text_en: Before you head towards the canal, unfold the site plan so north is at the top. You're at the southern entrance, and the information point is directly ahead; the courtyard is where several paths join. The canal forms the northern boundary. Some of you may remember the site before restoration, but the routes have changed, so please use today's plan. And don't take a shortcut over the low fencing: the bank can be slippery even when it looks dry.

Our first hands-on activity takes place in the workshop shelter. From the entrance, turn immediately left and follow the short path into the south-west corner. It is before you reach the central courtyard, so don't carry heavy tools all the way to the canal. The shelter has a wide roof and benches where volunteers will show how traditional lock gates were maintained.

The bird hide is the quietest stop on the plan. From the central courtyard head towards the canal, then take the path to the far left, ending in the north-west corner. Please keep conversations low there. Kingfishers are occasionally spotted near the reeds, but the main purpose is to let visitors notice how birds use different parts of the waterway without disturbing them.

Our temporary water testing lab is at the north-east end of the grounds. Walk from the courtyard towards the canal and turn right at the top of the path. You'll find a tent in the far right corner, opposite the bird hide. Staff demonstrate how cloudy water is measured, and explain why a single sample tells us less than a series collected across several weeks.

For first aid, don't go back to the entrance unless you are already close to it. The first-aid tent is just east of the central courtyard, at the middle-right side of the plan. There are volunteers there throughout the day. We can help with minor cuts, provide drinking water and contact the emergency services if someone needs more specialised medical care.

The restored boat exhibit occupies the south-east corner, on the right-hand branch of the path from the entrance. It's not the newer training boat beside the information board. The exhibit boat is the wooden vessel with its interior opened for viewing, so visitors can see how cargo was packed below deck and how little space the crew had.

Across the day, we have twelve demonstration sessions. Six are introductory talks, and the others are short practical sessions. The printed leaflet still says ten because two extra volunteers offered to run workshops. Check the noticeboard for the latest order: we may swap a session if the wind becomes too strong near the exposed canal bank.

The first demonstration of the working lock gate begins at eleven twenty. You may hear someone mention eleven o'clock, but that is when the operators check the mechanism and clear the safety barrier. Watching the preparation is interesting, yet the explanation for visitors starts twenty minutes later, once the public route has been secured.

Our volunteers wear blue badges. The orange badges on some jackets belong to contractors working on the site, so please don't assume those people can answer visitor questions. If you lose your group, approach a blue-badged volunteer and tell them the activity you were attending. They can direct you back without interrupting the work around the water.

For the nature survey, visitors should use the paper observation sheets provided at the information point. We tried a mobile form last year, but the signal is unreliable at the far end of the canal and several records were lost. You can photograph your sheet for yourself, but please hand the original to a volunteer before leaving.

Finally, the small bridge beside the old towpath is closed today. The towpath itself remains open as far as the viewing rail, but maintenance engineers found loose boards on the bridge yesterday. No one should cross it or try to take a shortcut through the neighbouring field. There are plenty of safe views of the canal from the official route.

If you've only managed two of the demonstrations, that isn't a failure. Spend a little time watching how the canal works, rather than rushing round to collect stamps. The information team can show you an accessible way back from wherever you finish, and we'll announce the closing arrangements over the site speakers. Any questions about the route before you go?

parts.title: Evaluating a Campus Food-Waste Pilot
parts.context: academic discussion among students and tutor

turns.text_en: Thanks for bringing the preliminary results. The university dining service wants to know whether the food-waste pilot actually changed behaviour, not just whether the posters were attractive. Let's be careful about what your evidence can support.

We observed the lunch area for two weeks. There are fewer trays left on tables, but the number of people using the dining hall also changed when exams began. I don't think our first chart tells the full story.
And some students moved to the outdoor seating area, which we couldn't see from our original observation point. So I agree that a simple count would give us a misleading conclusion.

The outcome we need to measure is food discarded, not satisfaction with the menu. The dining manager is interested in fewer leftovers, while the advertising team keeps asking about how many people noticed the campaign.
I can compare weighed leftovers from the same lunch service on matched days, rather than relying on how full the bins look at the end.
That's a stronger outcome because it is tied to actual waste. We'll explain the distinction clearly in the report.
Before we give the posters credit for the change, think about what else was happening on campus. Were there the same number of students eating there in both weeks?
The exam timetable is the most important one. Fewer students were on campus during the second week, so naturally there was less food left in total.
We can use the number of meals served to adjust the figures, although that doesn't completely remove the effect of different student routines.
You submitted photographs of bins as your main evidence. What concerns me is that a photograph shows volume, not weight; light packaging can make a bin look full without much food in it.
We thought the visual contrast would be easy for readers to understand, but I see that photographs alone don't support a numerical claim.
We could use them merely to illustrate the site, provided we don't imply they measure food waste.
Was anything else altered in the cafeteria during the pilot? Even a sensible operational change can affect the outcome.
The serving team introduced smaller portion sizes on three days. That could reduce leftovers regardless of the posters, even if students' intentions didn't change.
So we'll record those days separately. Otherwise we might credit the communication campaign for an effect produced by the kitchen.
Don't present only the total weight from each week. We need a measure that remains meaningful when visitor numbers differ.
We'll report food discarded per meal served, then include the total as supporting context. That makes the comparison more defensible.
And we should state the uncertainty rather than pretending a two-week trial proves long-term behaviour change.

Now assign a method to each unanswered question. First, why are students leaving food? A short anonymous diary would let people record what happened immediately after lunch without an interviewer judging them.
That's preferable to collecting names, especially when students might feel embarrassed about admitting they wasted a meal.
We'll keep the diary questions brief and avoid asking about health or personal circumstances that aren't needed.
For queue and tray-return behaviour, use an observation grid with predetermined categories. Free-form notes would be difficult to compare across observers.
We can mark where people leave trays and whether bins are visible from different tables, without recording anyone's identity.
I'll test the grid with another observer so we know whether both of us interpret the categories in the same way.
To understand kitchen operations, we should interview staff. They know when portions, serving times or ingredients changed, and that context won't appear in student surveys.
I'll arrange staff interviews outside the busy lunch period and ask about procedures rather than individual performance.
Good. Make it clear that employees won't be identified in the public write-up.
For the actual waste measure, use weighed samples of the food remaining after selected lunch services. The kitchen can separate edible leftovers from packaging using a standard procedure.
I'll check that the scales are calibrated and record the measurement time, because wet waste can change weight if it sits for hours.
We should also photograph the measurement setup for our methods appendix, but not treat those pictures as the data.
Finally, to see whether any change persists, we'll use a follow-up survey several weeks after the posters have been removed.
That won't prove causation, but it may reveal whether students remember the message and report different habits later.
Exactly. Frame it as exploratory evidence and keep it separate from the measured results of the original pilot.

The report will be more convincing if it acknowledges the limits of the pilot. We can explain what improved in the measurement method and what needs a longer trial, rather than announcing success too early.
I'll rewrite the introduction so the main outcome is obvious from the first paragraph, and I'll put the adjusted chart beside the raw totals.
And I'll prepare the ethics note and method checklist. We can then compare the evidence without confusing a campaign with a confirmed behavioural change.

parts.title: What Tree Rings Can — and Cannot — Tell Us

turns.text_en: What can a tree trunk tell us about weather long before local measurements began? A tree is not a recording instrument in the ordinary sense: it responds to weather, soil, competition and damage all at once. The scientific task is therefore to compare many samples, test the timing of each pattern and avoid assuming that one unusually narrow ring proves a particular historical event. I'll start with how wood is formed, then explain how researchers build a shared timeline, and finally consider the limits of the evidence.

New wood is produced by a thin living layer called the cambium, situated between the bark and the older wood. Cells formed there gradually become part of the trunk. The width of the new wood is influenced by growing conditions, but it is not a simple thermometer. A warm year might help growth in one location while causing water stress in another, and the age of a tree also affects how much new wood it produces.

In many temperate species, growth begins with relatively large cells that carry water efficiently. This lighter-looking part of a ring is known as earlywood. Later in the season the cell structure often changes. When a slice of wood is polished and observed under good light, the contrast can help researchers distinguish one growth cycle from the next, although some trees in tropical environments do not form such clearly recognisable annual boundaries.

The denser material produced towards the end of the growing season is called latewood. Its cells generally have thicker walls and smaller spaces inside. The change from earlywood to latewood creates a visible pattern, but researchers must distinguish a true annual boundary from an interruption caused by a brief dry spell. That is one reason samples are examined carefully under a microscope rather than counted from a casual photograph.

Climate is only one influence on ring width. Competition from neighbouring trees can reduce the light, water and nutrients available to an individual trunk. Suppose a tree becomes much wider after a nearby tree falls: the change might reflect a new gap in the canopy, not an improvement in regional rainfall. Researchers therefore pay attention to the position and history of each tree before interpreting its rings as environmental evidence.

The central technique for assigning reliable years is crossdating. Instead of simply counting backwards from the bark, scientists line up patterns of wide and narrow rings from several trees, looking for the same sequence in different samples. A ring that appears missing in one tree may be visible in another. This matching process is particularly important when studying old timber from a building whose original cutting date is uncertain.

A period of drought can produce exceptionally narrow rings in trees whose growth is limited by available water. Yet even a striking pattern must be compared with rainfall records, soil conditions and other samples. A different species growing beside a stream may show a weaker response. Researchers talk about the strength of a statistical relationship, not about a universal code in which every narrow ring always represents the same weather event.

Scientists sometimes move beyond ring width and examine stable isotopes in the wood. The balance between forms of an element can reflect aspects of water use or environmental conditions during growth. Such chemical evidence can add another perspective, but it requires careful preparation and specialised instruments. The interpretation still depends on the species, local climate and how the measured signal is influenced by physiological processes inside the tree.

Some trees survive surface fires and retain visible fire scars in their trunks. When these injuries can be dated using surrounding rings, they help researchers reconstruct the timing of burning at a site. This does not mean every fire leaves a scar or that each scar represents a large regional event. The absence of a mark is not proof that no fire occurred; survival, tree species and the intensity of the fire all affect the record.

By combining overlapping sequences from living trees, fallen trunks and historically used timber, a team can construct a regional chronology. It provides a longer shared timeline against which new samples can be compared. The most reliable chronologies use many independent pieces of wood, transparent dating procedures and checks for unexpected gaps. Their value lies in agreement across samples rather than the apparently impressive age of one individual tree.

Finally, every reconstruction needs an explicit account of uncertainty. A ring pattern can support a proposed sequence without revealing the exact temperature of a particular afternoon centuries ago. Researchers may report confidence intervals, differences between sites or alternative interpretations. Good scientific communication explains which claims are strongly supported, which are tentative and which questions tree-ring evidence cannot answer without help from other historical or environmental records.

The central message is that tree rings are useful because they can be dated and compared, not because each ring tells a complete story on its own. When several kinds of evidence are combined, the record can reveal environmental patterns over timescales longer than modern instruments have been operating. But any interpretation must respect the biological complexity of the tree and the possibility that the same pattern has more than one cause.
